title: Judge imposes sweeping emergency order halting DOJ pressure campaign on election officials across the country
content: A federal judge imposed a sweeping emergency order halting various aggressive tactics employed by the Trump administration in recent days to pressure election officials across the country. “Although Defendants claim that their actions are designed to halt unlawful voting by noncitizens, their actions are likely to have the effect of interfering with election administration and disenfranchising lawful voters,” US District Judge Trina Thompson said in her opinion granting a temporary restraining order Friday evening. She said, while her order is in place, the Justice Department and the Department of Homeland Security cannot demand that election officials in any state segregate ballots, purge voters from voter rolls, or halt ballot processing. Thompson, who was appointed by President Joe Biden, is also blocking threats of criminal prosecutions against election officials from those agencies and said that the administration cannot take other actions that “threaten, intimidate or coerce” election officials to demand changes in ballot processing procedures on claims the voters are ineligible. Thompson’s opinion rebuked claims the administration has made for months that it can and will prosecute election officials for not doing enough to prevent illegal voting. “When state and local government employees perform the work of distributing, processing, or counting ballots or otherwise administering the 2026 midterm election” in accordance with the law, “they do not violate federal criminal law even if a particular ballot belongs to a registered voter alleged by Defendants to be ineligible to vote,” she wrote. She is also requiring the administration inform her of any “search warrant applications, grand jury subpoenas, or other demands to access election materials or ballots” that have been issued related to lists the administration has created to allege individuals are ineligible to vote. The judge set her order to expire November 16. CNN has reached out to the Justice Department for comment. The case was brought in the Northern District of California — a court known to lean left — by a coalition of labor unions and civil rights groups, including the NAACP and the League of United Latin American Citizens. They allege the administration’s recent conduct violates the Voting Rights Act and amounts to an unconstitutional intrusion into state control over election administration. Central to the administration’s efforts is a controversial data-matching operation DHS has spearheaded that has compared state voter lists with federal records. Election officials say the lists of suspected noncitizens DHS has created using the program are unreliable and include US citizens. Several judges are now scrutinizing that approach in cases brought in recent weeks. The Trump administration’s aggressive efforts have increasingly run aground in the courts — as the federal government attempts to force states to cooperate with the push it says is aimed at preventing noncitizens from voting. Despite lawsuits, the Justice Department has sought to increase pressure, sending letters to 29 states and Washington, DC, threatening investigations and demanding that they preserve records and voter data from the 2024 election. Federal law already requires jurisdictions to preserve records for 22 months after an election. In California, where the Justice Department has sued to try to block the counting of ballots of thousands of voters that the federal government says may be noncitizens, a federal appeals court has rejected the administration’s demands. The 9th US Circuit Court of Appeals said the administration doesn’t have the right to intervene in how the states verify citizenship status. CNN’s Evan Perez contributed to this report. This story has been updated with additional details.

title: How one billionaire could ‘singlehandedly’ alter the course of the midterms
content: Elon Musk has plowed nearly half a billion dollars into elections in the 2026 cycle, a spending spree that makes him the single, largest disclosed donor in modern American politics and one of the Republican Party’s largest-ever benefactors. The world’s richest man has contributed more than $445 million to federal committees alone through mid-October – more than double the nearly $177 million that Democratic megadonor George Soros gave to outside groups during the 2022 cycle to become the largest known individual donor in the last midterm elections for Congress. Musk’s money could “single-handedly” alter the course of the midterms, said Brendan Glavin, who oversees research at the nonprofit OpenSecrets. The group tracks political spending. “One person is completely dominating and changing the landscape of how Republicans are able to spend money and defend themselves,” he said. Musk has donated nearly $216 million to America PAC, the super PAC at the center of his political operation. The group’s activity spans more than 40 House and Senate races this fall, according to federal campaign data. But nowhere has the billionaire spent more than in Texas, where he lives and has headquartered parts of his business empire. The key Senate contest there between Democrat James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton could determine which party controls the chamber during the last two years of President Donald Trump’s tenure in the White House. America PAC has funded mailers, digital advertising and other outreach to Texas voters in an effort to defeat Talarico and other Democrats. But far more Musk money – at least $168 million so far – has been deployed in Texas through other groups. A pair of donations last month, for instance, from the SpaceX CEO to the Senate Leadership Fund, a leading Republican super PAC, were quickly funneled to a second group, Texas PAC, that has issued blistering attacks against Talarico on the airwaves, recent disclosures show. Much of the anti-Talarico messaging seeks to portray him as out of step with Texas values, with some citing his vote as a state legislator against a 2023 law banning gender surgeries and other medical interventions for minors. (Talarico’s campaign has said he does not support gender surgery for children but opposed the bill because it was overly broad.) Musk also has donated $10 million to the pro-Paxton Lone Star Liberty PAC, which as CNN’s KFILE reported this week, has underwritten AI-generated robocalls attacking Talarico. A spokesperson for Musk’s America PAC declined to comment. But Republicans familiar with the strategy said the PAC is broadly focused on helping the GOP retain control of Congress next year and describe Musk’s move to shoulder some of the Texas advertising costs as freeing other GOP groups to deploy resources elsewhere to protect the Senate majority. In a statement, the Senate Leadership Fund’s executive director Alex Latcham said the donors who stepped up to fund Texas PAC “ensured that we did not have to divert any resources from other key races” and have allowed the group “to run effective campaigns across the map.” Talarico has raised more money than any other federal candidate this cycle, $146 million through October 14, more than six times the $22.3 million collected by Paxton, according to Federal Election Commission records . And a CNN poll released Thursday shows the Democrat with a narrow lead over Paxton. But Talarico has faced an onslaught of outside spending from pro-Paxton interests, including those funded by Musk, in recent weeks. In the final four weeks of the Texas Senate campaign, Democrats have been outspent by Republicans on ads by more than 2 to 1, $118.9 million to $54.7 million, according to AdImpact data. Dave Carney, a top political adviser to Texas GOP Gov. Greg Abbott’s reelection campaign, says Republicans in the state believe the spending by Musk and other GOP groups is starting to exact a toll on Talarico. “It has taken the pretty boy, neighbor next door, cute moderate nice guy and has exposed his voting record,” Carney told CNN this week. Talarico is increasingly taking aim at Musk to highlight his outsized role in the Texas race, as Democrats work to motivate their voters to turn out in the final stretch. “Elon Musk is trying to buy this Senate seat,” Talarico said during a recent rally as he ticked off the breadth of Musk-funded activity in the state. “In all likelihood, if you’ve seen an attack ad on your TV, that was Elon,” he said. “If you’ve gotten lies in your mailbox, that was Elon. If you’ve received a text message saying scary things about me, that was Elon, too.” A recent digital ad from Talarico reinforced the message, saying Paxton “will owe him everything” if Musk’s money helps to elect the Republican. A Paxton spokesperson did not respond to CNN’s inquiry. Democrats have sought to use Musk as a foil to spur turnout before. In Wisconsin last year, a $20 million spending blitz by Musk and aligned groups – along with his decision to campaign in the state – became a central message for Democrats who soundly defeated Musk’s preferred candidate in a state Supreme Court contest. Other Democratic ads that year used images of Musk holding a chainsaw aloft to highlight his controversial and short-lived tenure running the Trump administration’s Department of Government Efficiency. This year, Musk has kept a lower profile, even as his political spending has soared to new heights. He has not campaigned with candidates. But he has used X, the social media platform he controls to amplify his criticism of Talarico with increasing frequency. In the last week, he’s posted more than a dozen times about the Democrat, often disparaging him as “far-left extremist.” Musk and his spending loom large over the election, said Lynda Tran, a Democratic strategist based in Washington. The billionaire may not be on stage “wielding a chainsaw and other theatrics,” she said, “but there’s no way to hide the ball on the contributions he’s making or how much he cares about various Republican races.” CNN’s David Wright contributed to this report.

title: They strangled us, says founder of Russian newspaper shut under pressure from authorities
content:
At the editorial offices of Novaya Gazeta, they are packing up and shutting down.
Everywhere I look there are cardboard boxes and plastic bags. Everything must go.
For thirty years this has been Russia's most prominent independent newspaper, featuring investigative journalism fiercely critical of those in power.
Now Novaya Gazeta is being evicted from its home of three decades. The paper also says it's been blocked from receiving donations.
It's accusing the Russian authorities of killing it off.
"There are different ways to commit murder," journalist and co-founder of the paper Dmitry Muratov tells me. "They chose to strangle us."
"First, they blocked our websites and banned the paper edition. Then they revoked our media licence. One by one we were declared 'foreign agents', and our journalists were attacked.
"Now we can't earn any more money. The banks are refusing to accept donations from our readers. In our country there are political repressions going on. Those have reached us."
In 2021, Muratov was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize for efforts "to safeguard freedom of expression, a precondition for democracy and lasting peace".
The award didn't stop the Russian authorities from designating him a 'foreign agent' in 2023. The label is often used to punish critics of the government.
Over the years Novaya Gazeta had developed a reputation for fearless investigative reporting on subjects such as corruption, human rights violations and abuse of power by officials and bureaucrats - dangerous topics in Russia.
The paper says that six colleagues were killed for "fulfilling their professional and civic duty". Those journalists include Anna Politkovskaya, who was shot dead in the stairwell of her apartment block twenty years ago this month. She had written extensively on the wars in Chechnya.
As I walk down a corridor, I spot the office Anna had used. Following her killing, the room and all the items in it were preserved and became a museum in her memory. Since the eviction order, most of the objects have already been removed. All that's left is the desk and, lying on top, a portrait of Anna.
In a statement on its website announcing the closure, Novaya Gazeta launched a stinging attack on the Russian authorities.
"They've killed us," it starts. "The newspaper is no more. The Russian authorities and Russian special services have forced the paper to stop its work."
The publication claims it is the victim of "a coordinated act" and blames "the repressive state apparatus".
"Human rights and freedoms have been eliminated in the country and their protection has been equated to a crime… The courts have been destroyed along with the law. Having personal convictions is now state treason."
Since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022, the pressure on independent journalism and independent Russian journalists has been growing.
Soon after the start of what the Kremlin calls the 'special military operation', new laws were adopted in Russia. Their aim: to punish dissent and silence criticism of the war and of those in power.
Earlier this year there was a police search of Novaya Gazeta's editorial office. A veteran investigative journalist Oleg Roldugin was arrested and charged with "unlawful access to computerised information".
ranking_reason: Novaya Gazeta's closure and accusations of political pressure from Russian authorities

analysis.reason: Novaya Gazeta's closure and accusations of political pressure from Russian authorities

final_quality.reason: This article reports a substantive and important development in the category of people, specifically the closure of a prominent independent Russian newspaper and the accusations of political pressure from authorities. The article provides clear reasons for readers to care, including the background on the newspaper's reputation for fearless investigative reporting and the impact of the closure on the journalists' ability to do their job.
